Dear Secretary Reese:

        The Midcontinent Independent System Operator, Inc. (“MISO”), through this filing,1
submits proposed revisions to its Open Access Transmission, Energy and Operating Reserve
Markets Tariff (“Tariff”),2 to establish a Large Load Addition Resource Study (“LARS”) process,3
associated application and operational requirements to enable load and generation to be studied
together leveraging existing MISO processes to facilitate the timely availability of the tool to
customers.4 The LARS proposal will help streamline the MISO generator and load interconnection
process by providing expedited review of the addition of 200 MW or greater loads together with
new generation resources that are electrically proximate to those loads. Through this coordinated
study framework, LARS is designed to facilitate the timely and reliable interconnection of Large
Loads and new generation onto the MISO system.

        MISO requests that the Tariff revisions submitted herewith be made effective December 2,
2026, which is not less than sixty (60) days nor more than one-hundred and twenty (120) days
from the date of this filing. MISO requests that the Commission issue an order by this date in
order to allow MISO to commence the first LARS Study Period in Q1 of 2027. As discussed
below and in the supporting testimony of Christina Drake,5 action is needed in the near term to
enhance the available tools to address the reliability impacts associated with the impending
interconnection of Load, including the anticipated interconnection of significant large loads.

    I.    EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

        LARS responds to rapidly evolving reliability and resource adequacy needs in the MISO
region. MISO is proposing LARS to facilitate the cost effective, timely and reliable integration of
new large loads into the system. LARS supports the Commission’s call to action to meet these
new challenges in short order. LARS will provide a path for the interconnection of both large
loads and supporting generation pairs in a parallel 120-day study process. The proposal leverages
the existing success in the MISO’s Expedited Project Review (“EPR”) process on the load side
and lessons learned from Expedited Resource Additions Study (“ERAS”) process on the
generation side.

       MISO is experiencing significant growth in electricity demand at the same time that
additional resources are needed to reliably serve that demand. MISO projects annual load growth
of approximately 1% to 3% through 2044, driven in part by energy-intensive loads such as data
centers and manufacturing expansion, and has identified the need to accelerate new resource
additions as demand grows.6

        The need to accelerate the infrastructure necessary to reliably serve growing electricity
demand is also reflected in the Department of Energy’s (“DOE”) Speed to Power initiative, which
seeks to accelerate development timelines for large-scale transmission and generation projects to
meet rising electricity demand.7 LARS advances that objective within the MISO region by
providing a process through which significant new large loads and generation intended to support
that load can be studied on an accelerated and coordinated basis.

        LARS is also responsive to the Commission’s June 18, 2026, Order Instituting Proceeding
Under Section 206 of the Federal Power Act in Docket No. EL26-70-000 (“Show Cause Order”).
The Commission preliminarily found, among other things, that MISO’s existing Tariff may be
unjust and unreasonable because it does not provide generator interconnection study procedures
and services that account for the operational dynamics of serving electrically proximate large
loads.8 The Commission specifically addressed the potential for a new generating facility and an
electrically proximate large load to be studied in a manner that accounts for their combined
transmission system impacts.9 LARS provides a mechanism for MISO to study a large load and
the generation that will serve it at the same time such that their combined transmission system
impacts may be considered together.

        In addition, the Commission requested a detailed informational report on any proposals
under consideration to address the issue of resource adequacy to serve new large loads, strongly
encouraging new proposals to the extent necessary to address these concerns.10 The LARS process
responds to this concern and serves to provide a critical tool that allows the timely integration of
resources associated with these new loads supporting regional resource adequacy. While MISO’s
existing processes have been sufficient to ensure resource adequacy in the short term, the unique
commercial and operational characteristics of new large loads and the speed with which they need
to come online have prompted MISO to develop LARS as an additional tool to further support
resource adequacy as new large loads are integrated into the MISO region in the future.

        This proposal is deliberately tailored to significant new large loads. MISO initially
proposed a minimum eligibility threshold of 250 MW and expressly sought stakeholder input
regarding whether that threshold appropriately captured high-impact loads without unnecessarily
expanding the scope of the process.11 MISO set the initial threshold at 250 MW as recent EPR
results showed that large loads of 250 MW and greater created meaningful grid impacts, with
upgrades becoming increasingly likely between 300–500 MW and consistently necessary at 1,200
MW and above with multi-element upgrades. Stakeholders proposed alternative thresholds,
including 200 MW, which MISO proposes herein as it expands the LARS proposal beyond
hyperscale load to apply to other kinds of large loads including industrial loads.12

       Importantly, LARS is designed to work in concert with other MISO large load initiatives,
such as MISO’s proposed Zero Injection Generator Interconnection Agreement (“ZGIA”)13 and
Interconnection Reliability Requirement (“IRR”)14 frameworks currently pending before the
Commission and maintains protections for generation already progressing through MISO’s
generator interconnection queue or more commonly known as the Definitive Planning Phase
(“DPP”) process. LARS provides a different tool for large load interconnection arrangements
involving paired generation that do not fit within the ZGIA framework.

        Taken LARS provides MISO with a targeted tool to address the intersection of significant
large load additions, optimized Network Upgrades with generation and load, generation
development, and supports resource adequacy. The proposal allows MISO to study qualifying
load and associated generation on a coordinated basis, responds to issues identified in the
Commission’s Show Cause Order, and is designed to preserve the integrity of MISO’s existing
generator interconnection processes. LARS is needed now to facilitate the cost-effective and
reliable interconnection of impending new large loads and generation additions on an accelerated
timeline.

 II.       OVERVIEW OF THE LARS PROCESS

           A.     BACKGROUND

        The MISO region is experiencing a significant change in both the magnitude and pace of
anticipated electricity demand. MISO’s 2026 Reliability Imperative explains that, following a
period in which electricity demand grew at an average annual rate of approximately 0.5% between
2009 and 2024, MISO now projects annual load growth of approximately 1% to 3% through
2044.15 MISO identifies energy-intensive loads, including data centers and manufacturing
expansion, among the sources of this sustained and concentrated growth.16

       This growth has corresponding implications for the resources necessary to maintain
operational reliability and resource adequacy. MISO has stated that, as demand grows rapidly,
maintaining existing resources and accelerating new resource additions are critical.17 MISO’s
2026 Planning Resource Auction results likewise recognize that, although the region has sufficient
resources to satisfy resource adequacy requirements for the 2026-2027 Planning Year, faster

resource additions remain necessary to support large-load growth and ensure resource adequacy.18
MISO has, therefore, identified rapid load growth as a core component of its broader Reliability
Imperative. MISO’s Transmission Evolution work specifically identifies the need to “speed up
timelines for new generation and transmission projects” while managing large-load growth without
compromising reliability.19

        Against this backdrop, the challenge presented by new large load growth is not limited to
connecting the load itself. Significant new demand must be accompanied by sufficient resources
to maintain reliability and resource adequacy. MISO’s Large Load Working Group (“LLWG”)
was established to address this broader relationship, with a mission encompassing markets, reliable
operations, planning, and resource adequacy associated with the integration and enablement of
large loads.20 LARS is intended to address one aspect of that challenge by establishing a process
through which qualifying Large Load additions and associated new generation can be studied on
a coordinated basis. Studying qualifying load and generation together, with aligned study timeline,
provides a mechanism for MISO to consider significant new demand and the resources associated
resulting in optimized network upgrades. In this manner, LARS is designed to facilitate the reliable
integration of significant new load and generation on an accelerated timeline.

         B.       STRUCTURE OF LARS AND PARTIES

        LARS provides a parallel study process for a proposed large load and generation pair.21 As
MISO explained in its motion for abeyance, “LARS will assess the transmission infrastructure
needed to meet new large loads and new generation in an efficient process that can be executed on
a shorter timeline, further supplementing the opportunities available for members to facilitate new
large spot loads effectively.”22 The generation and load studies will be completed at the same time
and will finish within approximately 120 days. To allow this to happen, LARS brings the
requirements that are needed for both the generation and load studies under a common application,

the LARS Application and provides a framework for participation by the entities involved in the
existing MISO processes that LARS builds upon.

       There are four primary types of entities involved in implementing LARS aside from MISO.
These are the LARS Associated Transmission Customer, the Interconnection Customer(s) who will
own or operate the Generating Facility, the applicable Transmission Owner, and the
owner/controller of the ultimate load (called the “LARS Associated Load”). To understand how
LARS will work, a brief explanation of each of these parties’ roles in the process is provided below.

        The first of these parties is the LARS Associated Transmission Customer.23 This is the
entity that procures Transmission Service for load and has a direct relationship with the load. This
is often a Load Serving Entity (“LSE”). Because only the Transmission Customer can procure
Transmission Service under established Tariff processes, LARS requires the LARS Associated
Transmission Customer to be the party that initiates the LARS Application and obtains the
resulting Transmission Service.24 Ultimately, the LARS Associated Transmission Customer acts
as a coordinator between the other entities involved in the LARS process.

         Second, there is the Interconnection Customer. This is the entity that will complete the
section of the LARS Application that supports the generation portion of the LARS study, will be
responsible for meeting the requirements of Attachment X pertaining to the generation study, and
will receive Interconnection Service under an LLGIA. The Interconnection Customer can be any
entity (including an Independent Power Producer (“IPP”)) whose Generating Facility will provide
Energy for the LARS Associated Load provided it is permitted by applicable laws and regulations
to do so.25 The Interconnection Customer has the contractual relationships required by LARS to
show that the Generating Facility is in fact paired with the LARS Associated Load.26

        Third, the Transmission Owner owns the facilities the LARS Associated Load will connect
to the Transmission System. The Transmission Owner works with the other parties to establish
the Point of Interconnection (“POI”) for the Generating Facility(ies) and the Point of Withdrawal

        The fourth key participant is the entity that owns or controls the LARS Associated Load,
which for purpose of LARS must be a large load of at least 200 MW.28 While MISO usually will
not have a direct relationship with this entity and does not purport through this filing to impose
obligations directly on them, this entity will have a crucial role in establishing relationships
between the parties directly involved in LARS, in supplying information necessary to complete
the LARS Application, and study process, and in enabling the other parties to meet their obligations
under LARS.

        As noted above, the roles of these parties and their specific responsibilities reflect existing
Tariff requirements and practices. LARS does not seek to fundamentally change the established
roles of the entities participating in the load and generation studies but rather seeks to coordinate
them. LARS thus provides for faster and more transparent interconnection arrangements for large
loads with paired generation, while offering customers speed-to-power, optimized transmission
solutions, and greater certainty to support siting, and financing of large load projects. The outcome
of the LARS process is MTEP approval of transmission required to reliably facilitate the
withdrawal of the load and corresponding injection rights for the proposed generation. The
component parts of the process are discussed in greater detail below.

         C.       THE LARS APPLICATION

        MISO is establishing a single application process for the participants in the LARS process.
The LARS Application will be a single submission consisting of materials required by Attachment
FF for the load and Attachment X for the generation.29 Because LARS involves two separate study
processes being completed concurrently and in parallel, all the relevant parties to the load and
generation pairing must apply together.30 While the LARS Application process may only be
initiated by the LARS Associated Transmission Customer, the Interconnection Customer, the
Transmission Owner, and the LARS Associated Load customer must all complete the required
information as part of the application before it will be reviewed by MISO. Independent Power
Producers and other kinds of Interconnection Customers are not prohibited from participating in

the LARS process.31 The LARS Application will also serve as a repository for all information
required by the load and generation study processes. A non-refundable fee of $250,000 must

        Notably, MISO is establishing a “pre-submission coordination process” that LARS
applicants must participate in prior to submitting a LARS Application.33 This coordination process
requires the potential LARS Interconnection Customer and the Transmission Owner to meet and
agree on a definitive Point of Interconnection for the proposed LARS Generating Facility. Forty-
five days prior to a LARS Application deadline, a potential LARS Interconnection Customer must
notify the Transmission Owner to whose Transmission Facilities the potential LARS
Interconnection Customer proposes to Interconnect of its plans to participate in LARS. After
receiving a request to meet from any potential LARS Interconnection Customer, the Transmission
Owner must meet with them and any other impacted parties necessary to determine a definitive
POI within ten business days after receiving a request for the meeting. The parties must jointly
agree on a feasible POI no later than ten business days prior to the next LARS Application deadline
as published on MISO’s website. An attestation from the Transmission Owner stating that it has
an agreed POI with the LARS Interconnection Customer(s) must be included in the LARS
Application.34

        MISO is proposing these pre-submission coordination activities for several reasons. First,
while the LARS Associated Transmission Customer is the only party that may submit the LARS
Application, MISO is requiring that they actively participate in the LARS process with the
potential LARS Interconnection Customers prior to LARS Application deadline. Second,
requiring pre-submission coordination activities will increase the efficiency of reviewing the
LARS Application with all the relevant parties identified, the agreed upon POI identified, and other
necessary details have already been determined by the time the LARS Application is submitted to
MISO. Having the LARS Application parties agree on many of these necessary details in advance
of submission will also help avoid future disagreements or changes, which can lead to unnecessary
or late withdrawals from the study process. MISO has heard from stakeholders and learned from
experience that an accelerated study process requires that the relevant participants have
coordinated and agreed upon key details (such as the location of the POI) up front and not after
they have submitted their application. Third, requiring coordination meetings between these parties
will assist them with identifying any other relevant parties who may need to participate in the
LARS process. Ms. Drake explains that to effectively facilitate the speed of the LARS study
process, MISO needs all relevant parties to the load and generation pair to not only be identified
at the outset but committed to working together.35

       MISO will accept LARS Applications on a rolling basis, and the applications will be
queued on a serial, time-stamped basis based on time of submission to the LARS process. There
will be three LARS study periods each year and each study period will be completed in
approximately 120 days, as explained by Ms. Drake.36 MISO will accept ten LARS Applications
per study period and the LARS Applications will be assigned to study periods in order of
submission. Customers interested in joining the next LARS study period must submit their LARS
Application to MISO no later than 20 business days prior to the scheduled kick-off of the LARS
study period as published on the MISO public website. MISO will keep an open queue of LARS
Applications and will replace any LARS Application that withdraw prior to study kick off with the
next submitted generation/load pair not included in the current study period. Once the LARS study
process has kicked off for a specific LARS generation/load pair, then that spot is lost for the LARS
study period it is part of even if the pair later withdraws during the study process.37

        An Interconnection Request included in a LARS Application must be accompanied by an
executed agreement between the Interconnection Customer and either the LARS Associated
Tranmission Customer or the entity that owns or controls the LARS Associated Load. The
agreement must demonstrate that the output of the LARS Generating Facility will serve the LARS
Associated Load. The agreement must be legally binding and must state a minimum term of five
years so that if any transmission solutions need to be developed, there is sufficient time to work
through the processes for development. As described in Section 3.12.2(i) of Attachment X, the
agreement must be in the form of a power purchase agreement (“PPA”) or similar off-take
agreement, a Build-Own-Transfer Agreement, or any other kind of agreement used by Load
Serving Entities including a special contract, a large load tariff agreement, or a retail service
agreement. Ms. Drake explains that in response to stakeholder feedback, MISO revised the Tariff
redlines to explicitly state the agreement can be executed between the generator and large load. 38
This does not supersede the role of the LARS Associated Transmission Customer to determine
whether to submit a LARS Application but does allow flexibility for different types of agreements
that are consistent with state law and supported by the parties.39 MISO also added the third
agreement option to incorporate specific utility arrangements with large loads that are not
traditional PPAs to link the generation and load.40

        Other requirements of the LARS Application include limiting the Interconnection Requests
to NRIS, limiting the amount of requested Interconnection Service to no more than 150% of the
peak demand of the LARS Associated Load, and demonstration of 100% site control for the POI
including a one-line diagram demonstrating the Generating Facilities and any associated electrical
equipment required.41 Based on stakeholder feedback MISO established the 150% of
Interconnection Service limitation to ensure the generation is required to reliably serve the load
within the same LRZ. As Ms. Drake states, MISO sought to establish a closer connection between
what is needed by the LARS Associated Load and what is being proposed by the LARS
Interconnection Customer.42 Thus, MISO implemented this requirement to directly connect the
Generating Facility with the LARS Associated Load and to allow for different generator fuel types
and accreditation. Ms. Drake explains that “this requirement establishes a clear connection
between the output of the Generating Facility and the load without being overly prescriptive on
generation fuel type, dispatch requirements, or other operational considerations.”43

        Another important condition of the LARS process is the requirement that the load and
generation pair be located in the same Local Resource Zone (“LRZ”).44 The Point of
Interconnection(s) specified in a LARS Application must be located in the same LRZ as the Point
of Withdrawal (“POW”) of the LARS Associated Load. As discussed by Ms. Drake, the intent of
the LARS process is to identify an optimized Network Upgrade solution for both the load and
generation, and MISO retains that flexibility in the LRZ because it aligns with MISO’s Resource
Adequacy construct.45 Specifically, MISO does not have a requirement that loads bring generation,
but through the proposed LARS process, by restricting the Point of Interconnection(s) specified in
a LARS Application to be located in the same LRZ as the Point of Withdrawal, MISO providing
an incentive for Load to bring Generation in a manner that maximizes the positive impact this
Generation has on Resource Adequacy. MISO recognizes there are other ways it could have
limited the pairing such as requiring the generation and LARS Associated Load to be located in
the same Local Balancing Authority area or through requiring that the location of the Generating
Facilities be within a specific number of substations of the LARS Associated Load. However,
limiting the pairing of Generating Facilities and LARS Associated Load to the same LRZ strikes
an appropriate balance between accommodating large, landlocked LARS Associated Loads that
may need additional POIs to propose sufficient Generating Facilities needed to serve that load.
Limiting the proximity of the Generating Facilities and LARS Associated Load provides a solution

         MISO is proposing to increase flexibility in the LARS process by allowing a LARS
Associated Load to be served by multiple Generating Facilities under specific circumstances.
First, all Generating Facilities serving a LARS Associated Load must be included and identified
in the same LARS Application and must request a minimum of 200 MW of Generator
Interconnection Service in aggregate. Second, a LARS Associated Load may be served by more
than one group of Generating Facilities located at different POIs, but a separate LARS Application
must be submitted for each POI group of Generating Facilities. Stated differently, each group of
aggregated LARS Generating Facilities at a single POI must submit a separate LARS Application.
Each LARS Application must identify the total amount of load requested by the LARS Associated
Load and must identify every Generating Facility providing power to that load.46 While MISO is
allowing aggregation for LARS Generating Facilities, MISO is not allowing aggregated load to
participate in LARS. As explained earlier, MISO developed LARS in the context of dramatic large
load growth and created the LARS process to help address that growth. Ms. Drake explains that
limiting LARS load participants to at least 200 MW at one POW ensures that the load coming
online is sufficiently large to warrant inclusion in LARS and is not a large group of small loads
banded together.47

         While the LARS Application requirements are expected to reduce the number of
speculative projects submitting applications, they provide enough flexibility to enable these large
loads to connect to the system. As Ms. Drake explains in her testimony, ensuring that only
commercially viable and shovel ready projects enter LARS is a necessary prerequisite to running
these extremely fast serial studies because each LARS study must be able to rely on the Network
Upgrades resulting from previously completed LARS study actually being developed.48 Thus, the
strict entry requirements for LARS both support its intended benefits while also underscoring that
LARS is not, and should not be, a replacement for the DPP.49 Rather, it is intended to be a narrowly
scoped but powerful process.

         E.          COORDINATED LARS STUDY PROCESS

        The LARS process builds off the existing EPR and ERAS processes but improves upon
them by integrating planned load with the generation, which enables the identification of more
optimal Network Upgrades. If MISO knows a large load is coming, which it will in the LARS
process, then MISO can study the load’s impacts with greater certainty and reduce the risk of
speculative generation or load. By running the generation and load studies in parallel, MISO is
able to review constraints identified on both the load and generation sides and can see the impacts
to the system with each different configuration. This information can then inform the transmission
network upgrades that are solutions for the transmission needs identified in the load and generation
studies. MISO can also bring Sugar-developed solutions to the Transmission Owner and
Interconnection Customer for coordination.67

        The goal of LARS is not necessarily to find the lowest cost solution for either the load or
generation but to identify the solution that best fits both the generation and load needs at the lowest
cost. MISO expects LARS to produce more cost-effective solutions that are more efficient for the
grid overall.68 This allows MISO to combine solutions between the load and generation side for
more optimal, efficient, and effective responses. MISO can then come up with more effective
solutions to help integrate load and generation into the system, which maximizes the benefits of
both study processes and reduces integration costs. Thus, as Ms. Drake explains, the LARS
process enables MISO to optimize solutions for the transmission grid to reduce costs overall while
also maintaining reliability.69

III.   THE PROPOSED REVISIONS ARE JUST AND REASONABLE

        The LARS proposal and its corresponding Tariff changes are just and reasonable. LARS
provides a valuable tool to enable the study of LARS Associated Loads that are brought to MISO
with a paired generation solution. LARS meets the urgent need for an accelerated evaluation
process that accounts for both load and generation, responds to concerns identified in the Show
Cause order regarding proximity between large loads and their associated generation, and does not
disturb existing DPP processes. The LARS process is not unduly discriminatory to any potential
market participant and respects existing roles and responsibilities. LARS brings together several
independent MISO processes needed to integrate a new large load. Through the LARS
Application, MISO has established a framework that allows different stakeholders to proactively
coordinate the addition of these generation/load pairs onto the system. The result is an accelerated
process that allows for the integration of generation/load pairs and optimized transmission
solutions.

alternative to MISO’s ordinary generator interconnection process. Together with the ZGIA
framework, LARS provides MISO with an additional mechanism to facilitate the development of
resources needed to support significant new load growth while maintaining reliability and
appropriate protections for existing Interconnection Customers.

        If the LARS Associated Load ceases service within the first fifteen years, then the
Generating Facility will have up to one year to acquire new Interconnection Service. MISO added
this provision in response to stakeholder concerns that the termination of the relationship between
the LARS Associated Load and the Generating Facility (either through termination of their
agreement or the LARS Associated Load discontinuing operations) could leave an otherwise useful
Generating Facility suddenly without Interconnection Service and unable to serve other Load
needs. If the LARS Associated Load withdraws from LARS in the first fifteen years, then its
paired Generating Facility will be subject to AERIS and the QOL processes and will have up to
one year to obtain Interconnection Service through the MISO DPP process. If the Generating
Facility is unable to obtain new Interconnection Service within one year, then the LLGIA will be
terminated. This is necessary to avoid any resource adequacy concerns that might be implicated
by immediately terminating the LLGIA and provides flexibility for the Generating Facility to
continue operating until it can be utilized in a different MISO process.

        If the LARS Associated Load ceases service after the first fifteen years of being formally
paired, then it is reasonable to allow the Generating Facility to continue to utilize the
Interconnection Service granted through the LLGIA. Several stakeholders expressed concern that
a permanent pairing requirement would strand a Generating Facility that had a remaining useful
service life even if such Generating Facility could be used—or was needed—to address resource
adequacy needs following the departure of the LARS Associated Load. MISO added this language
in response to these stakeholders’ legitimate concerns that Generating Facilities submitted to
LARS in good faith and that had served LARS Associated Loads for long periods of time should
not be forced to go offline or undergo a second study process with potentially significant new costs
if the LARS Associated Load unexpectedly ceased operations.

         Thus, MISO is requiring the generation and load to remain paired for fifteen years because
it provides important safeguards that prevent customers from misusing the LARS process to obtain
Interconnection Service and only serve the LARS Associated Load for a short period of time.
Fifteen years is also a reasonable time period as reflected in many standard large load contracts
and sufficient to deter entities from invoking the needs of a specific large load as a pretext to bypass
the DPP queue and receive immediate and unrestricted service. This language clearly allows the
Generating Facility to continue operating under the terms of the LLGIA after fifteen years have
passed even if the LARS Associated Load ceases use of its Transmission Service. This provides
the Generating Facilities with certainty after the fifteen-year period has passed and allows for these
facilities to continue assisting with any resource adequacy needs that may be occurring at that time.

This section was necessary to add to Attachment FF because the LARS Application must contain

Attachment FF that it will have one single review period to identify any deficiencies in the LARS
Application and the applicants will have one single cure period to address those deficiencies. That
is necessary to ensure that LARS process only lasts approximately 120 days. MISO cannot be
delayed by numerous deficiency and cure periods.

These provisions describe situations where a generating solution does not yet have a GIA on file
with the Commission and indicates that it may be considered as an alternative transmission
solution in the LARS load study if: (1) a valid Interconnection Request for such Generating Facility
has been submitted for processing under the LARS process specified by Attachment X to the Tariff;
and (2) the Transmission Provider has received an executed agreement between the LARS
Interconnection Customer, the entity(ies) with the LARS Associated Load with a minimum of 200
MW, and the LARS Associated Transmission Customer that satisfies the requirements of
Attachment X, Section 3.12.2(i). The provisions also explain that if the LARS Associated Load’s
in-service date is prior to the COD of the Generating Facility, then MISO can: 1) require the LSE
to delay the in-service date of the LARS Associated Load until such time as an alternative solution
can be placed in service or the Generating Facilities achieve(s) COD in accordance with Section
I.D.1.b.ii of this Attachment; or (2) impose operational limitations on the LARS Associated Load
that MISO deems are reasonably necessary to maintain the reliability of the Transmission System
until such time as the Generating Facility achieves Commercial Operation or an alternative
solution is placed into service.

 V.       THE LARS STAKEHOLDER PROCESS

         MISO developed LARS through an iterative stakeholder process focused on the
relationship between significant new load, associated generation, and the need to maintain system
reliability. The LLWG itself is charged with addressing large-load issues across markets, reliable
operations, planning, and resource adequacy.100 Stakeholders first raised the need to coordinate
large load and generator interconnection studies through MISO’s issue process.101 In early January
2026, MISO convened a Large Load Additions Workshop where it presented its forecast of large
load additions, which showed large load additions escalating sharply over the next several years,
driven primarily by data centers, and noted that federal policy supporting artificial intelligence was
accelerating near-term growth.102

         Large loads continued to be a significant topic of conversation in all of MISO’s stakeholder
meetings. To provide a dedicated forum for large load matters, MISO’s Steering Committee
approved a charter for the Large Load Working Group.103 The LLWG reports to MISO’s Advisory
Committee and is chartered to provide input and policy guidance to MISO Management and the
Advisory Committee on market, reliability, planning, and resource adequacy matters related to the
integration of large loads within the MISO footprint. The LLWG held its first meeting on April
20, 2026.104 In its first several meetings, the LLWG took up the large load interconnection
reliability requirements (LLWG-2026 3), reserve product enhancements for large load (LLWG-
2026-2), Firm Service Step Up for large load interconnections (LLWG-2026-1), and the ZGIA
(PAC-2024-4B), each of which forms part of the broader large load framework within which LARS
was developed.105

Tariff remains just and reasonable without provisions tailored to large loads, or to propose Tariff

        As a result of stakeholder feedback, MISO changed the LARS process minimum Large
Load value to be 200 MW instead of 250 MW. Stakeholders proposed a range of approaches to
the threshold. The July LLWG stakeholder record includes a recommendation to reduce the
minimum threshold from 250 MW to 200 MW to capture projects sufficiently large to warrant
coordinated load-generation evaluation while maintaining the proposal’s focus on projects with
significant system impacts.115 Other stakeholders supported retaining a minimum-MW
mechanism to limit the process to high-impact large loads.116 MISO made this change based on
significant stakeholder feedback that many emerging data center and large industrial projects in
the 200-250 MW range can have significant system impacts and would benefit from the
coordinated study process. Lowering the threshold also allows access to the LARS framework
while maintaining its focus on large, impactful load additions. The 200 MW minimum threshold
strikes the right balance between different kinds of large load and hyperscalers.

        At the September 23, 2026, LLWG meeting, MISO presented the final proposed LARS
process and updated tariff language for Attachement FF, Attachment X and associated Appendices
in response to the September 10th feedback. MISO explained that it had changed the minimum
threshold LARS Associated Load size to 200 MW (from the proposed 250 MW), allowed multiple
Generating Facilities to group at different POIs for one LARS Associated Load, and added a new
contract agreement option for LSEs. MISO also clarified several of the requirements of the LARS
process including addressing the concerns on representation of the LARS generator/load pair
within the parallel study processes.117

project-readiness requirements, study assumptions, and the interaction between LARS and the
existing Generator Interconnection Queue.118 The resulting LARS proposal reflects MISO’s effort

to establish a targeted process for significant new load additions while coordinating the study of

        MISO submits that the Tariff revisions proposed in this filing establish a just, reasonable,
and not unduly discriminatory mechanism for rapidly integrated large loads with paired generation.
The Tariff revisions are limited in scope and in impact but offer significant benefits in terms of
improving the coordination between load and generation studies to reflect the joint impact of both
the generation and the load it will serve, and avoiding negative impacts to other MISO processes
and the stakeholders who participate in them. As proposed, LARS is both a powerful tool for
responding to urgent industry needs as well as a tailored solution with safeguards sufficient to
guard against overuse of the process. The benefits of LARS are not free. Both the Interconnection
Customer and LARS Associated Transmission Customer are required to undertake commitments
that exceed those imposed on Interconnection Customers in the DPP. These additional
commitments and risk are necessary to provide the certainty that allows LARS to move at an
expedited pace without negative impacts to other processes. The LARS process is open to all
Interconnection Customers that meet the Tariff’s requirements and that are willing to accept the
greater commitments and limitations imposed by LARS.

          Assessment Study as set forth in Section 3.7.2.2 of the GIP.

          Study and Reliability Assessment Study and share results with the Interconnection
          Customer within one hundred eighty (180) Calendar Days of the request.

          The Reliability Assessment Study for the time period between the date that the Existing

          Generating Facility shall evaluate the performance of the Transmission System to

          may include stability analysis as necessary. The Existing Generating Facility shall be
          responsible for mitigating any reliability violation identified in the Reliability Assessment
          Study and may not cease operations until all mitigations are implemented or are in
          service. Mitigation for this interim period may, as applicable, include: (i)

                   GENERATOR INTERCONNECTION PROCEDURES (GIP)



   SECTION 1. DEFINITIONS.


          10 kW Inverter Process shall mean the procedure for evaluating an Interconnection
   Request for a certified inverter-based Small Generating Facility no larger than 10 kW that uses
   the screen set forth in Section 14.


           Adverse System Impact shall mean the negative effects due to technical or operational
   limits on conductors or equipment being exceeded that may compromise the safety and
   reliability of the electric system.


           Affected System(s) shall mean an electric transmission system or the electric system
   associated with an Existing Generating Facility or of a higher queued Generating Facility, which
   is an electric system other than the Transmission Provider’s Transmission System that is affected
   by the Interconnection Request. An Affected System may or may not be subject to FERC
   jurisdiction.


           Affected System Interconnection Customer shall mean any entity that submits an
   interconnection request for a Generating Facility to a transmission system other than
   Transmission Provider’s Transmission System that may cause the need for Affected System
   Network Upgrades on the Transmission Provider’s Transmission System.


           Affected System Network Upgrades shall mean the additions, modifications, and
   upgrades to Transmission Provider’s Transmission System required to accommodate Affected
   System Interconnection Customer’s proposed interconnection to a transmission system other
   than Transmission Provider’s Transmission System.

                 pertaining to a Generating Facility. The GIP specifically applies when one of the
                 following is proposed by an Interconnection Customer: (i) a new Generating
                 Facility at a new Point of Interconnection that does not meet the criteria set forth
                 in Sections 2.1 (b) or (c), (ii) additional generation at an existing Point of

          Planning Phase I), and section 7.2.1.3 (Transmission Provider Review of Site Control
          Sufficiency). Notwithstanding the preceding requirements and upon written consent of

          During the Customer Engagement Window, the Transmission Provider shall establish a

          Transmission Owner must attend the Scoping Meeting. Transmission Provider shall use
          Reasonable Efforts to include any other Affected System Operators in the Scoping
          Meeting.


          The purpose of the Scoping Meeting shall be to discuss alternative interconnection
          options, to exchange information including any transmission data that would reasonably
          be expected to impact such interconnection options, to analyze such information and to
          determine the potential feasible Points of Interconnection. For purposes of clustering
          Interconnection Requests, Transmission Provider or Transmission Owner may propose
          changes to the requested Point of Interconnection to facilitate efficient interconnection of
          Interconnection Customers at common Point(s) of Interconnection. The requesting
          Transmission Provider or Transmission Owner shall notify Interconnection Customers in
          writing of any intended changes to the requested Point of Interconnection within two (2)
          Business Days after the conclusion of the Scoping Meeting, and the Point of
          Interconnection shall only change upon mutual agreement. Transmission Provider,
          Transmission Owner and Interconnection Customer or MHVDC Connection Customer

          (iv) general voltage issues including voltage and frequency ride-through capabilities for

          3.7.2   Evaluation Process for Generating Facility Replacement Requests.
          The Transmission Provider will evaluate Generating Facility Replacement requests in the
          order in which they are submitted. The evaluation will consist of two studies: i) a

          Assessment Study as set forth in Section 3.7.2.2 of the GIP.

          Study and Reliability Assessment Study and share results with the Interconnection
          Customer within one hundred eighty (180) Calendar Days of the request.

          3.7.2.2 Generating Facility Replacement—Reliability Assessment Study
          The Reliability Assessment Study for the time period between the date that the Existing
          Generating Facility ceases commercial operations and the Commercial Operation Date

          Generating Facility shall evaluate the performance of the Transmission System to
          determine if thermal and/or voltage violations of applicable the Electric Reliability
          Organization Standards and Transmission Owner planning criteria are caused by
          removing the Existing Generating Facility from service prior to the Commercial

          conditions on the Transmission System that would exist if the Existing Generating
          Facility is taken offline to the conditions on the Transmission System as they exist when
          the Existing Generating Facility is online. The scope of Reliability Assessment Study
          may include stability analysis as necessary. The Existing Generating Facility shall be
          responsible for mitigating any reliability violation identified in the Reliability Assessment
          Study and may not cease operations until all mitigations are implemented or are in
          service. Mitigation for this interim period may, as applicable, include: (i)

                       UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                              BEFORE THE
                FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION

                    PREPARED DIRECT TESTIMONY OF

                DIRECTOR, GENERATION INTERCONNECTION
                                                                                     Tab C
                                                                                     Page 1


 1           I.      PROFESSIONAL BACKGROUND AND QUALIFICATIONS

 2   Q.   PLEASE STATE YOUR NAME, BUSINESS ADDRESS, AND RELATIONSHIP TO

 3        THE MIDCONTINENT INDEPENDENT SYSTEM OPERATOR, INC.

 4   A.   My name is Christina Drake. I am the Director, Generation Interconnection for the

 5        Midcontinent Independent System Operator, Inc. (“MISO”). My business address is 720

 6        City Center Drive, Carmel, IN 46032.

 7   Q.   PLEASE BRIEFLY DESCRIBE YOUR EDUCATION AND PROFESSIONAL

 8        BACKGROUND.

 9   A.   I hold a Bachelor of Science in Electrical Engineering from Rose-Hulman Institute of

10        Technology, and a Master of Business Administration (“MBA”) from Anderson

11        University. I have been employed by MISO since 2002 in a variety of different roles. I

12        spent the first 17 years of my career in various positions in MISO Operations. During that

13        time, I worked as a North American Electric Reliability Corporation (“NERC”) certified

14        system operator in engineering and as reliability coordinator in MISO’s control room. I

15        also led several groups within MISO Operations as a manager in engineering, operations

16        processes and controls, and generation interchange. I’ve served in control-room operations

17        and leadership across markets and planning, and I now lead Generation Interconnection

18        strategy and execution for the region. I previously led Economic, Interregional & Policy

19        Planning in transmission planning, including development of MISO’s 20-year Future

20        Scenarios and support for the $20B Long Range Transmission Planning portfolio. My

21        background spans reliability coordination, operations engineering, settlements, and more

22        than 15 years of people leadership across real-time operations, markets, and transmission

23        and resource planning.
                                                                                      Tab C
                                                                                      Page 2

 1   Q.   PLEASE DESCRIBE YOUR CURRENT ROLE AND RESPONSIBILITIES.

 2   A.   As the Director of Generation Interconnection, I am responsible for the administration of

 3        MISO’s Generator Interconnection Procedures (“GIP”), which are set forth in Attachment

 4        X of MISO’s Open Access Transmission, Energy and Operating Reserve Markets Tariff

 5        (“Tariff” or “MISO Tariff”). I oversee MISO’s Interconnection Queue, known as the

 6        Definitive Planning Phase (“DPP”), including the negotiation and execution of Generator

 7        Interconnection Agreements (“GIAs”), which are based on MISO’s pro forma GIA set

 8        forth in Appendix 6 of the GIP. I also oversee the group that manages and processes the

 9        temporary Expedited Resource Addition Study (“ERAS”) process, and will also oversee

10        the group that will manage the generation studies related to Large Load Resource Addition

11        Study (“LARS”) process. I have been directly involved in the preparation and development

12        of the current proposals.

10   Q.   WHAT IS MISO’S TRANSMISSION STUDY PROCESS FOR LARS?

11   A.   MISO studies load and generation in a cumulative impact to make sure there is a reliability

12        plan for any load and generation moving forward. First, MISO will complete a load model

13        build with the proposed LARS generators. Then MISO will review the proposed LARS

14        projects with reliability assumptions and determine if any constraints are identified. This

15        process includes reviewing the outage of the generator in the study. After completing a

16        load and generation constraint review, MISO will determine whether there are any common

17        issues solutions. A planning level solution is established at the end of the load study

18        process.

19        In the LARS load study, since the system is so interconnected, MISO is looking at

20        cumulative load additions to the system, which helps it ensure the reliability of the system

21        overall. Viewing and studying load additions from a cumulative perspective produces

22        study results that generate multiple scenarios and ways to see multiple impacts on the

23        system, thereby providing a complete picture of any potential impacts on the system.

20                     IV.    LARS AND FERC’S SHOW CAUSE ORDER

21   Q.   IS THE LARS PROCESS RESPONSIVE TO FERC’S SHOW CAUSE ORDER?

22   A.   Yes. LARS is responsive to the Commission’s Show Cause Order. The Commission

23        preliminarily found, among other things, that MISO’s existing Tariff may be unjust and
                                                                                         Tab C

 1        unreasonable because it does not provide generator interconnection study procedures and

 2        services that account for the operational dynamics of serving electrically proximate large

 3        loads. The Commission specifically addressed the potential for a new generating facility

 4        and an electrically proximate large load to be studied in a manner that accounts for their

 5        combined transmission system impacts. LARS provides a mechanism for MISO to study

 6        generation and load at the same time such that their combined transmission system impacts

 7        may be considered together.

 8   Q.   HOW DOES LARS ADDRESS FERC’S SHOW CAUSE ORDER?

 9   A.   LARS addresses the concerns identified in the Commission’s Show Cause Order by

10        establishing a coordinated and accelerated process for studying qualifying large loads and

11        the new generation associated with them. Rather than studying the load and generation

12        independently and sequentially, LARS allows MISO to evaluate the load, associated

13        generation, and necessary transmission solutions on parallel tracks using a coordinated

14        system representation. As explained earlier in my testimony, this enables MISO to

15        consider the combined transmission system impacts of the proposed configuration while

16        addressing the distinct reliability considerations applicable to both the load and generation.

17        LARS also addresses the need for timely interconnection of new generation needed to serve

18        new large loads. By coordinating the load and generation studies within an accelerated

19        study cycle, LARS is designed to provide greater speed and certainty regarding the

20        transmission solutions necessary to reliably integrate both components. At the same time,

21        LARS is designed to preserve the integrity of MISO’s DPP process and avoid providing

22        an avenue for new generation to circumvent existing interconnection processes. In this

23        way, LARS provides a targeted mechanism to address the interconnection issues associated
                                                                                        Tab C
                                                                                       Page 40

 1        with the speed of large load growth and considerations surrounding proximately located

 2        generation and load as identified in the Show Cause Order.

 3   Q.   HOW      DOES       LARS      ADDRESS        THE     ELECTRICALLY            PROXIMATE

 4        REQUIREMENT IN THE SHOW CAUSE ORDER?

 5   A.   MISO’s LARS proposal provides the Tariff structure necessary to enable an

 6        Interconnection Customer to serve an electrically proximate load as the LARS Associated

 7        Load must be located within the same LRZ. MISO did not want to limit the pairing of

 8        generation with associated load to a specific number of substations because that would

 9        limit how MISO may optimize common solutions. In MISO, anchoring the proximate

10        requirement with the LRZ is more efficient and effective because it enables more

11        generation to serve a single load across a broader geographic area but in a manner that still

12        addresses resource adequacy and reliability of the system.         Ultimately, limiting the

13        generation and LARS Associated Load to locations within the same LRZ ensures

14        deliverability of the generation to the LARS Associated Load because it avoids potential

15        capacity import / capacity export limitations for the individual LRZ and also avoids price

16        separation between the paired generation and LARS Associated Load.

17        Moreover, allowing Generating Facilities participating in LARS to interconnect at multiple

18        POIs provides a “proximate plus” solution for the pairing of load with generation. This

19        provides Interconnection Customers with the necessary flexibility to serve extremely large

20        loads and in way that MISO can optimize any necessary transmission solutions. This

21        structure also reflects stakeholder feedback regarding the need to accommodate the

22        interconnection of large, landlocked loads that may need additional POIs to propose

23        sufficient generating facilities to meet the load.
